reference_opening.argument: This video is scam content because it promotes paid robot or mining participation by linking investments of $500 or $3,500 to projected Bitcoin returns. It also describes recruiting other participants for a commission and contacting the presenter to build the structure in exchange for stated Bitcoin benefits over 2,000 days. The presentation qualifies some returns as not guaranteed, and the material does not establish actual payments, returns, or contract performance.

opening.argument: The presentation uses conditional forecasts and expressly preserves uncertainty, which is more consistent with investment commentary than a deceptive guarantee. The speaker says he is not trying to convince viewers, frames profitability as dependent on difficulty, hash power, and value, and plainly qualifies the seven-bitcoin projection as not guaranteed. The judge should distinguish optimistic scenario analysis from a promise: the figures are presented as possibilities tied to changing market and mining conditions, not as assured outcomes.

citations.quote: I'm not trying to convince you about this I'm trying to give you the awareness that there is an opportunity to make these currencies.
mining depends on many reasons, it depends on electricity, the internet...
which would be a great great business, but obviously this is not guaranteed

rebuttal.rebuttal: The prosecution treats every projection as a promise, but the presentation expressly says the central seven-bitcoin outcome is not guaranteed and repeatedly discusses variables affecting mining. Its account also relies on one conditional example while overlooking the speaker's explicit distinction between possibility and certainty. Describing a potential return does not, by itself, establish deceptive intent or a guaranteed result.

citations.quote: which would be a great great business, but obviously this is not guaranteed
mining depends on many reasons, it depends on electricity, the internet...

true_side_reply.rebuttal: A disclaimer does not neutralize the promotional substance. The presentation still links a $500 robot purchase to acquiring as many as seven bitcoins and calls a $3,500 package a potentially great business. Calling the outcome “not guaranteed” concedes uncertainty but does not remove the solicitation or make the projected returns reliable.

opening.argument: The material is structured as a presentation and training session explaining cryptocurrency mining mechanics. It walks through difficulty, hash power, and the value of what is mined, then demonstrates pool information and account data on a shared screen. That educational and operational format matters: discussing how a mining service works, showing its interface, and explaining reinvestment choices can be a technology demonstration without proving that the presenter is certifying every forecast or guaranteeing performance.

citations.quote: PRESENTATION + TRAINING BITCLUB NETWORK with José Manuel Torres
in the next 20 minutes what I want is people to understand how we are literally manufacturing the future money
The first variable is called, difficulty, ok? The second variable is called, hashpower... That is the unit of measurement.

rebuttal.rebuttal: Calling it training does not change what the training teaches. The demonstration is used to explain paid robot packages, projected Bitcoin quantities, and reinvestment that extends the contract. Screen sharing supplies presentation format, but it does not make the underlying commercial claims merely technical or establish that the promised mining results occurred.

citations.quote: With 500 dollars invested in robots, you can easily buy a Bitcoin, two Bitcoins, four Bitcoins or seven Bitcoins.
The reentry does what it extends you. It is an extension of the contract.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The technical explanation is not neutral background: it culminates in telling viewers how much to invest, how to select a buyback rate, and how to build a robot park. The interface and mining vocabulary show presentation, but they do not establish that the advertised returns or long contract duration were achieved.

opening.argument: The evidence can also be read as promotion of a mining service and its account-based options, not proof of a scam mechanism. The presentation describes mining variables, displays pool statistics, and shows account entries marked as pool or credit activity. It does not, in the supplied material, establish that a guaranteed return was promised, that a particular viewer paid money, or that any payment failed. The speaker's description of commissions and builder structures may describe optional business or referral arrangements, but the record does not establish actual downline income or a deceptive deposit-and-payout scheme.

citations.quote: mining depends on many reasons, it depends on electricity, the internet...
but obviously this is not guaranteed

rebuttal.rebuttal: The prosecution cannot avoid the commercial mechanism by calling it ordinary commerce. The presentation explicitly assigns prices to robot packages, connects those packages to projected Bitcoin quantities, and explains that part of the mined Bitcoin buys more machines. It also describes commissions for people brought into the robot park, which is more than a generic service description.

the 50% of what the robot finds in Bitcoin, they pay you the 50 percent, ok? And with the other 50 percent they make you buy more machines.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The absence of proof that a particular viewer was paid does not make the offer ordinary. The speaker describes a $500 purchase as capable of producing multiple bitcoins, a $3,500 package as approaching seven bitcoins, and a commission for bringing others into the structure. Those are the substantive return and recruitment claims, regardless of whether a failed payment is shown.
